papers.title: Sustained mindfulness practice and socio-professional factors predict quality of life improvement in cancer patients: the Onco-MBSR study.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: MBSR is increasingly integrated into supportive cancer care and has demonstrated beneficial effects on quality of life (QoL) and psychological distress. However, determinants of individual response to MBSR remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to identify predictors of QoL improvement following participation in a standardized MBSR program among cancer patients. METHODS: This prospective, multicenter observational study included adult cancer patients enrolled in an 8-week standardized MBSR program across 12 certified centers in France and Belgium. QoL was assessed with EORTC QLQ-C30 and psychological distress with HADS at baseline (BL), end of program, and 3 months after program completion (M3). QoL improvement predictors between BL and M3 were explored using univariate analyses followed by multivariate models focusing on emotional (EF) and socio-family functioning (SFF). RESULTS: Among 211 participants with complete follow-up, significant improvements were observed across several QoL domains, particularly EF and SFF. In multivariate analyses, weekly mindfulness practice exceeding 50 min was the most consistent and robust independent predictor of improvement in both domains. Age was independently associated with EF, with poorer outcomes observed in participants aged 50-70 years. Socio-professional category (SPC) independently predicted SFF, with reduced improvement among craftsmen and blue-collar workers. CONCLUSION: In this large, real-world multicenter cohort, sustained engagement in mindfulness practice was the primary determinant of QoL improvement following MBSR in patients with cancer, while SPC and age modulated specific psychosocial outcomes. These findings support the need to promote long-term practice and adapt MBSR delivery to improve accessibility and effectiveness within supportive cancer care.
